brief.setting: Surgical ward, on a chest drain manikin
brief.role: Core surgical trainee, supervised by the respiratory registrar
brief.scenario: Mr Gareth Lowe, 67, is on day 5 after a right hemicolectomy and has a right pneumonia with a pleural effusion. A diagnostic tap gave turbid fluid, not frank pus, with pH 7.05. He weighs 78 kg. A Seldinger drain kit, ultrasound machine, local anaesthetic and an underwater seal bottle are provided.
brief.task: Insert a chest drain on the manikin, talking the examiner through each step, and answer questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Indication, consent, bleeding risk, scan, safe triangle, anaesthetise, aspirate, insert, secure, seal, X-ray.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Choosing a site by landmarks alone for fluid, or clamping a bubbling drain.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'll confirm his identity, the side, the indication and his consent."

grid.label: Indication and drain choice
grid.fail: Can't state why a drain is needed, or picks a large-bore drain by blunt dissection without a reason.
grid.pass: States pleural fluid pH 7.2 or less with no frank pus means a drain; chooses a small-bore drain, 14F or smaller.
grid.high: Adds that the drain goes in only if ultrasound shows enough accessible fluid to make it safe.

grid.label: Consent
grid.fail: Starts without consent or explains no risks.
grid.pass: Takes and documents informed consent: pain, bleeding, infection, drain falling out or blocking, failure, and rare organ injury.
grid.high: Quotes complications in 8–20% of insertions, and rechecks the decision immediately before starting.

grid.label: Bleeding risk
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about anticoagulants or clotting.
grid.pass: Checks anticoagulants, antiplatelets and a blood count; clotting only if anticoagulated or coagulopathic; prophylactic heparin and aspirin can continue.
grid.high: Knows the elective rules: warfarin stopped 5 days with INR 1.5 or less, DOAC stopped 24–48 hours; in an emergency, weighs the risk.

grid.label: Site: ultrasound and safe triangle (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Picks a site by landmarks alone, below the 5th intercostal space, posteriorly, or under the rib.
grid.pass: Scans at the bedside in the insertion position; site in the safe triangle, at or above the 5th intercostal space; needle just above the rib below.
grid.high: Names the borders: pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, the 5th intercostal space and the axilla; explains the neurovascular bundle runs under each rib.

grid.label: Local anaesthetic and aspiration
grid.fail: Injects without a dose limit, or advances the drain without aspirating fluid.
grid.borderline: Gives local anaesthetic safely but doesn't aspirate fluid before inserting the drain.
grid.pass: Plain lidocaine 1% within 3 mg/kg and never above 200 mg; infiltrates to the pleura; aspirates pleural fluid before going further.
grid.high: Calculates his limit: 3 mg/kg is 234 mg, so the 200 mg cap applies (20 ml of 1%); if no fluid is aspirated, stops and rescans rather than pressing on.

grid.label: Seldinger insertion and fixing
grid.fail: Uses a trocar, or pushes the dilator deep.
grid.pass: Needle, guidewire, dilator, then drain over the wire; holds the wire throughout; holding suture and dressing.
grid.high: Advances the dilator no more than 1 cm beyond the parietal pleura, and records the depth at the skin.

grid.label: Underwater seal and clamping (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Hangs the bottle above the chest, or clamps a bubbling drain.
grid.pass: Tube about 3 cm under water; bottle upright and below the insertion site; never clamps a bubbling drain.
grid.high: Controls effusion drainage: stop at 1,000 ml, restart after 1 hour at up to 500 ml per hour; clamps for cough or chest pain.

grid.label: Aftercare and documentation
grid.fail: Leaves without a chest X-ray or instructions.
grid.pass: Chest X-ray within a few hours; analgesia; procedure note with drain size, depth, sutures and fluid sent.
grid.high: Continuous observation for the first 15 minutes; written clamping and drainage instructions, flushes, and who to call.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Why does he need a drain?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's a big effusion, so I'll put in a large-bore tube to be safe.

fail.text: [Palpates and marks the 7th space, low in the chest, without scanning.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Injects local anaesthetic freely and passes the needle without aspirating.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Leaves once the drain is connected; no X-ray requested.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Turbid fluid with pH 7.05, below 7.2, so he needs a drain. For pleural infection, a small-bore Seldinger drain, 14F or smaller.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I've explained the risks: pain, bleeding, infection, the drain falling out or blocking, it not working, and rarely injury to lung or abdominal organs. He's signed the form.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Is he on anticoagulants or antiplatelets? What's his blood count? Prophylactic heparin can continue, and he needs clotting only if anticoagulated.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Scans him sitting as he'll be for the procedure.] Good pocket of fluid in the safe triangle, at the 5th space. I'll go just above the rib below.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Lidocaine 1%, keeping within 3 mg/kg and under 200 mg. [Infiltrates skin to pleura.] Fluid aspirated.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Needle, guidewire, dilator, drain over the wire, keeping hold of the wire; holding suture and dressing.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Connects to the bottle, tube under water, bottle below the chest.] If it bubbles, it must not be clamped.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Chest X-ray within a few hours, analgesia, and a procedure note with drain size, depth and sutures.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: pH 7.05 without frank pus means high risk of complicated infection, so a drain, as long as the scan shows enough accessible fluid. Small-bore, 12F Seldinger.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Consent covers pain, bleeding, infection, displacement, blockage and failure, and rarely organ injury; overall complications in 8 to 20%. I'll confirm he still agrees just before we start.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets? His morning enoxaparin is prophylactic, so it can continue. If he were on warfarin electively, I'd want INR 1.5 or less.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Scans him in position, then marks.] Safe triangle: lateral border of pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, the 5th space and the axilla. The vessels and nerve run under each rib, so I'll go just over the rib below.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He's 78 kg: 3 mg/kg is 234 mg, so the 200 mg maximum applies, 20 ml of 1%. [Infiltrates to the pleura.] Fluid aspirated; if it weren't, I'd stop and rescan.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Seldinger; dilator no more than 1 cm past the pleura; drain over the wire.] Holding suture, and I'll record the depth at the skin.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Tube about 3 cm under water, bottle upright and below him.] For this effusion: stop at 1,000 ml, restart after an hour at up to 500 ml an hour, and clamp if he coughs or gets chest pain.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Nurse to watch him continuously for 15 minutes. Chest X-ray within a few hours; flushes, analgesia, written drainage instructions and who to call.

failures.move: Inserting by landmarks alone for fluid, below the 5th intercostal space or posteriorly.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: risks liver, spleen or intercostal vessel injury, and a dry tap.
Safety-critical: the continuing air leak can cause a tension pneumothorax.

failures.move: Advancing the drain when no fluid was aspirated with the anaesthetic needle.
failures.consequence: The drain may enter lung, a solid organ or no fluid at all.

failures.move: Using a trocar, or advancing the dilator deep into the chest.
failures.consequence: Can puncture lung, heart or abdominal organs.

recovery.when: You're asked where without an ultrasound
recovery.line: For fluid I'd scan first; if no ultrasound were available, I'd defer unless it's an emergency.

recovery.when: The nurse wants to clamp for transfer
recovery.line: It's bubbling, so it stays unclamped, and the bottle travels below his chest.

knowledge.fact: Suspected pleural infection without frank pus: pH 7.2 or less means a drain if ultrasound shows enough fluid. Small-bore, 14F or smaller.
Safe triangle: lateral border of pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, the 5th intercostal space and the base of the axilla.
Ultrasound is mandatory for pleural fluid, in the position used for the procedure. Insert just above a rib; avoid posterior sites.
Large-bore drains for unstable trauma, haemothorax in an unstable patient, or a large air leak.
BTS: plain lidocaine 1% up to 3 mg/kg; the UK licence caps a single plain dose at 200 mg.
Lidocaine with adrenaline: maximum single dose 500 mg.
Uncontrolled effusion drainage has killed patients: observe continuously for 15 minutes and follow red-flag triggers for closing the drain.

recall.think: Organ puncture, bleeding, tension from a clamped drain, re-expansion oedema.
recall.say: "Ultrasound-guided, in the safe triangle, just above the rib."
do: Seal below the chest; never clamp if bubbling

numbers.meaning: plain lidocaine 1% (BTS dose, capped at the UK licensed maximum)
stop, then up to 500 ml/h after 1 hour

recall.trap: Clamping a bubbling drain for transfer.
recall.finish: Chest X-ray, observation, drainage instructions, documented.

sources.name: Roberts ME, Rahman NM, Maskell NA, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. Thorax 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1-s42
sources.supports: Suspected pleural infection without frank pus: immediate pleural fluid pH; pH 7.2 or less implies high risk and an intercostal drain should be inserted if the volume of accessible fluid on ultrasound makes it safe (strong, by consensus); initial drainage of pleural infection with a small-bore chest tube, 14F or smaller (conditional)

sources.name: Asciak R, Bedawi EO, Bhatnagar R, et al. British Thoracic Society Clinical Statement on pleural procedures. Thorax 2023;78(Suppl 3):s43-s68, with online appendices 4 and 8
sources.supports: Informed consent taken and documented before any pleural procedure, including recognised risks and failure; coagulation profile not needed without a history of coagulopathy or anticoagulants; chest drain complications 8-20%; elective: warfarin stopped 5 days with INR 1.5 or less, DOAC stopped 24-48 h, aspirin and prophylactic heparin can continue; emergency: weigh the bleeding risk; ultrasound mandatory before pleural fluid procedures (except emergencies), in the position the procedure is done; insert directly above a rib, in the triangle of safety, avoiding a posterior approach; lidocaine 1% up to 3 mg/kg (max 250 mg), with adrenaline up to 7 mg/kg (max 500 mg); aspirate fluid or air with the anaesthetic needle before insertion, and reassess if not; trocars avoided; small-bore drains (14F or less) usually Seldinger; large-bore for unstable trauma, haemothorax in an unstable patient or large air leak; dilator not more than 1 cm beyond the parietal pleura; holding suture for every drain; tube about 3 cm under water; bottle below the insertion site and upright; do not clamp a bubbling drain unless under specialist pleural supervision; controlled drainage: stop at 1,000 ml, restart after 1 hour at up to 500 ml per hour; continuous direct observation for the first 15 minutes; chest radiograph within a few hours; report depth, sutures, clamping instructions and who to contact

sources.name: NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde: Adult chest drain guideline, version 4
sources.supports: Triangle of safety: lateral edge of pectoralis major, lateral edge of latissimus dorsi, the line of the fifth intercostal space and the base of the axilla; thoracic ultrasound mandatory for pleural fluid procedures; dissection over the upper border of the rib; trocars never inserted; a bubbling drain must never be clamped; bottle below the insertion site and upright; chest X-ray after insertion

sources.name: NHS England National Patient Safety Alert NatPSA/2020/008/NHSPS: Deterioration due to rapid offload of pleural effusion fluid from chest drains
sources.supports: 16 incidents of harm (two deaths) in three years from uncontrolled or unmonitored drainage; controlled drainage per BTS; observation charts with continuous direct observation for the first 15 minutes and red-flag triggers for closing the drain

sources.name: Lidocaine 1% with adrenaline 1:200,000 solution for injection: Summary of Product Characteristics (emc 2397)
sources.supports: Maximum single dose of lidocaine given with adrenaline: 500 mg

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading

sources.name: Lidocaine Hydrochloride Injection BP 1% w/v: Summary of Product Characteristics (emc 6277)
sources.supports: Single doses of plain lidocaine (other than spinal) should not exceed 4.5 mg/kg (or 200 mg)

partner.opening: Please insert a chest drain on this manikin for Mr Lowe, talking me through what you're doing.

reveals.finding: He has capacity and agrees once risks are explained. Say: "Please tell him the risks."
Enoxaparin 40 mg prophylaxis at 08:00. No antiplatelets. INR 1.1, platelets 310.
Say: "A moderate right effusion with a few septations; deepest pocket in the mid-axillary line at the 5th space."
Say: "It's swinging, and 300 ml of turbid fluid has drained."

push.question: Why this site, and why above the rib?
push.expect: Safe triangle, ultrasound-guided; the intercostal vessels and nerve run under each rib.

push.question: What's the maximum local anaesthetic dose for him?
push.expect: Plain lidocaine 1% up to 3 mg/kg, not exceeding 200 mg: 200 mg (20 ml) at 78 kg.

push.question: How would you manage the drainage of this effusion?
push.expect: Stop at 1,000 ml, restart after 1 hour at up to 500 ml per hour; clamp for coughing or chest pain.

curveballs.prompt: No fluid comes back on the anaesthetic needle.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Stop and rescan; don't advance the drain.

curveballs.prompt: At transfer the drain is bubbling and the porter wants it clamped.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Never clamp a bubbling drain: keep it open, bottle below the chest.

curveballs.prompt: It's a trauma patient, shocked, with a large haemothorax.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Large-bore drain by blunt dissection, with the trauma team and senior help.

curveballs.prompt: After 800 ml he coughs repeatedly and his saturations fall.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Possible re-expansion pulmonary oedema: clamp, A to E, oxygen, urgent chest X-ray and senior review.
